chapters.summary: The prophet Ezekiel, by the river Chebar, sees the heavens opened and beholds a vision of God's glory and power, including the four living creatures and the wondrous wheels.
keyPoints: By the river Chebar, in the land of his exile, Ezekiel sees the heavens open and beholds a vision of God.
In the vision four living creatures appear, each with four faces and four wings, and a human likeness.
Beside the creatures are wheels within wheels, with rims so high they are awesome, moving as the spirit moved them.
chapters.application: When we feel lost in hardship, let us remember that God still reigns, and his glory far exceeds the limits of what we can see. Lord, open our eyes to see your presence and guidance even in ordinary life.

chapters.summary: God calls Ezekiel as a prophet, giving him his Spirit and a scroll, and sends him to speak God's word to rebellious Israel.
keyPoints: God's Spirit comes upon Ezekiel, setting him on his feet and enabling him to hear God's voice.
God sends Ezekiel to the rebellious house of Israel, to proclaim his word.
God warns Ezekiel not to be afraid, for though the people are rebellious, God will be with him.
chapters.application: When God calls you, do not be afraid because of hard circumstances or people's rejection - be strong in the Lord and faithfully proclaim the truth.

chapters.summary: The LORD calls Ezekiel to be a watchman, has him eat the scroll, gives him his message to deliver to the rebellious house, and promises to make him strong.
keyPoints: God gives Ezekiel a scroll to eat; it tastes sweet as honey in his mouth, symbolizing his receiving God's word.
God sends Ezekiel to the rebellious house of Israel; though they will not listen, God will make him strong.
God appoints Ezekiel a watchman, warning him that if he does not speak, the guilt will fall on him.
chapters.application: Let us receive God's word each day, faithfully proclaiming it even when we meet resistance, and stay watchful in fulfilling the duty entrusted to us.

chapters.summary: God commands Ezekiel to perform symbolic acts foretelling the siege of Jerusalem, and to bear the guilt of Israel and Judah.
keyPoints: He draws a city on a brick and lays siege to it, symbolizing Jerusalem's siege by Babylon.
He lies on his left side 390 days to bear Israel's guilt, and on his right side 40 days to bear Judah's guilt.
He eats limited and unclean food, foreshadowing the scarcity and defilement of the siege.
chapters.application: Let us stay watchful - though the consequences of sin are heavy, God still offers the chance to repent; may we turn from wickedness and live in holiness.

chapters.summary: God commands Ezekiel to shave his head with a sword, symbolizing the judgment and punishment Jerusalem will suffer for rebelling against God.
keyPoints: Through the imagery of shaving and scattering the hair, God declares that Jerusalem will suffer plague, famine, and sword.
Because Israel worshiped idols and broke the law, God's anger is kindled, and their punishment will be worse than that of the surrounding nations.
The purpose of judgment is that people may know the LORD is a righteous God, and take warning from it.
chapters.application: Let us examine whether we have strayed from God's way, and turn back in time, lest we bear the consequences of sin.

chapters.summary: God declares judgment on the idolatrous places of Israel; because they forsook God, they will suffer sword, famine, and plague, and be scattered among the nations.
keyPoints: God commands Ezekiel to set his face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy against their idol worship.
The idols and altars will be destroyed, the idol worshipers slain, their corpses cast before their idols.
The remnant, scattered among the nations, will remember God and loathe themselves for the detestable things they have done.
chapters.application: Let us turn away from the idols in our hearts and turn to the true God. In discipline, let us examine ourselves, turn back with a contrite heart, and experience God's mercy and restoration.

chapters.summary: This chapter declares that the end has come for Israel; because of their sin and detestable deeds, God will judge them according to their conduct, and none will escape.
keyPoints: God declares that the end has come for Israel, because the land is full of violence and detestable things.
The day of judgment draws near, and none can escape by silver or gold, for these cannot save them.
The temple will be defiled, the people punished for their sin, and the land filled with desolation and disaster.
chapters.application: Let us turn from wickedness and not trust in possessions; let us examine ourselves continually and stand in reverent awe before God, for judgment will surely come.

chapters.summary: In a vision Ezekiel sees the Jerusalem temple filled with idol worship, and God reveals that his glory is about to depart.
keyPoints: The prophet is carried in a vision to Jerusalem and sees detestable idols within the temple.
God points out that the elders of Israel worship idols in secret, provoking his anger.
The vision reveals that the people have turned away from God in heart and in deed alike, and judgment is coming.
chapters.application: Examine your heart for any hidden idols - money, status, or selfish desire - and repent and turn to God, for he sees all things.

chapters.summary: God commands his messengers to strike down every evildoer in Jerusalem, but marks and protects those who sigh and groan over the detestable things done in the city.
keyPoints: God summons the executioners of judgment, each with a weapon of destruction in hand.
God commands the man clothed in linen to put a mark on the foreheads of the righteous, and the killing begins at the sanctuary.
Judgment begins at God's house; those who sigh and groan are spared, but all the rest are struck down.
chapters.application: Even when wickedness fills the land, God still watches over those who grieve over sin. May we keep a sensitive heart, sighing over the injustice of the world, holding to holiness, and being remembered by God.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes the prophet Ezekiel's vision of God's glory departing from the temple, and the detailed vision of the cherubim and the wheels.
keyPoints: The appearing of God's glory and the vision of the cherubim
The structure and movement of the cherubim and the wheels
God's glory rises up from the temple and departs
chapters.application: When God seems to feel far away, examine your own conduct, and remember that he still reigns - his departure is only for a time, meant to lead us to repentance.

chapters.summary: In a vision God judges the leaders of Jerusalem, and promises that the exiles will return and receive a new heart, restoring their relationship with him.
keyPoints: God exposes the leaders' wicked schemes, declaring that the city will become a judgment pot, and they will be driven out.
The leaders are killed within the city; God scatters the people among the nations, yet becomes their sanctuary for a time.
God promises to gather Israel from the nations, give them a united new heart, and be their God.
themes: A New Heart and the Spirit
chapters.application: Even in hardship, God still cares for us; may we turn to him with a sincere heart, receive a new heart, and live a life of obedience.

chapters.summary: God commands Ezekiel to perform symbolic acts foretelling the siege of Jerusalem and the fate of King Zedekiah of Judah, showing that God's word will surely come to pass.
keyPoints: God has Ezekiel prepare an exile's baggage and move it before the people's eyes, symbolizing that the people of Judah will be carried into exile.
Ezekiel digs through the wall and carries out the baggage, foreshadowing King Zedekiah fleeing by night, only to be captured by the Babylonians.
God explains that these signs are meant to let the rebellious people know that the LORD reigns and fulfills his promises.
chapters.application: When God's word seems delayed, still trust in his promise, act in obedience in daily life, and wait for his work to be revealed.

chapters.summary: This chapter rebukes the false prophets and prophetesses, declaring that God will oppose their false prophecies and their deceptive ways.
keyPoints: The false prophets prophesy out of their own imagination, cunning as foxes, without having truly seen a vision.
They daub a flimsy wall with untempered mortar; their teaching of false peace will surely collapse.
God will set himself against the false prophets and prophetesses, cutting them off from among the people and saving his chosen ones.
chapters.application: Let us carefully discern what we hear, seek the truth, and not follow false peace, standing on God's word as our foundation and trusting the true God in adversity.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the LORD's answer to the elders of Israel who came to inquire of him: because they harbor idols in their hearts, they will be punished, and it stresses repentance and personal responsibility.
keyPoints: The LORD exposes the idols in the elders' hearts and refuses to answer their inquiry.
Though the prophet intercedes, the chosen people, because of their idolatry, will suffer four kinds of judgment.
The remnant that is saved shows forth God's righteousness and love, and calls the people to forsake their idols.
chapters.application: Examine your heart for any hidden idols, such as money, status, or selfish desire. Repent sincerely, forsake everything that takes God's place, and he will forgive us in his mercy and keep us walking in his way.

chapters.summary: This chapter uses the vine as a metaphor for Israel, showing it to be useless, since through its unfaithfulness it will be burned in the fire, symbolizing the coming destruction of Jerusalem.
keyPoints: Compared with other trees, the wood of the vine is useless, fit only for fuel.
Even when half the vine is burned, what remains is even more useless.
Because Israel has done evil and forsaken God, it will be burned in the fire like a useless vine.
chapters.application: Let us examine whether our lives bear fruit, lest we become a useless branch; let us stay abiding in Christ, bearing much fruit to glorify God.

chapters.summary: This chapter portrays Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife, recounting the grace shown to her, her turning to sin, and the punishment she receives, while promising ultimate restoration.
keyPoints: God chose and favored Jerusalem, like an abandoned infant taken in and raised, adorning her with beauty and honor.
Jerusalem relied on her beauty to commit whoredom and worship idols, becoming worse than Samaria and Sodom.
God will judge her in righteousness, yet remembers the covenant he made, so that through this covenant the people find forgiveness and restoration.
chapters.application: Let us always remember God's grace, never grow proud because of it, remain faithful in our devotion, turn away from idols, and when we fail, repent and turn back to God, for he shows grace according to his covenant.

chapters.summary: Using the parable of the two great eagles and the vine, this chapter declares that Judah, for breaking covenant and relying on Egypt, will bring judgment upon itself, but God promises that the house of David will one day be rebuilt.
keyPoints: The parable of the two eagles represents Babylon and Egypt, and the vine represents the royal house of Judah.
Judah broke its covenant with Babylon and turned to rely on Egypt instead, bringing disaster upon itself.
God promises to plant a tender sprig on the top of the cedar, foreshadowing the restoration of the messianic kingdom.
chapters.application: Let us keep our word and not rely on worldly power; trust that God provides a way through hardship, and that his promises will surely be fulfilled.

chapters.summary: Through a proverb and examples, this chapter sets forth God's righteous principle of judgment: each person is punished for their own sin, and whoever repents will live.
keyPoints: It corrects the misunderstanding of the proverb, 'The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge,' stressing personal responsibility.
It lists the standards of conduct for the righteous, the wicked, and the repentant, showing that God judges each according to their own deeds.
It declares that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but delights when the wicked turn from their evil way and live.
chapters.application: Do not shift the blame or dwell on the past; examine yourself, turn from wickedness in time, trust in God's mercy, and live a new life.

chapters.summary: This chapter, in the form of a lament, likens the princes of Judah to broken branches, brought down to ruin through their pride and rebellion.
keyPoints: The lioness represents the royal house of Judah; a young lion carried off to Egypt symbolizes the deposing of Jehoahaz.
Another young lion is led away to Babylon, referring to Jehoiachin being carried into exile as the nation's power wanes.
The vine is uprooted and its branches wither, showing that Judah has utterly lost its royal power and hope.
chapters.application: Let us humbly submit to God, not relying on power or ability; pride surely leads to a fall, and only through repentance and returning to God can we receive mercy and restoration.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the elders of Israel coming to inquire of the LORD; through Ezekiel, God reviews Israel's history, declaring that their repeated rebellion must be judged, yet promising their eventual return.
keyPoints: The elders of Israel come to inquire, but God refuses to answer, because their idols remain.
God recalls giving the law at the exodus from Egypt, but the people rebelled, and God withheld destruction for a time.
God declares judgment and discipline, but promises that the exiles will return and be made clean again.
chapters.application: Let us examine our hearts, remove every hidden idol, respond to God's call with sincere repentance, and be assured that he will grant us cleansing and restoration.

chapters.summary: Through Ezekiel, God declares that the king of Babylon will serve as the sword of God's judgment, striking Jerusalem and the Ammonites, showing forth his righteous judgment.
keyPoints: God has Ezekiel set his face toward Jerusalem and prophesy, declaring that God draws his sword from its sheath to judge the whole land.
The king of Babylon casts lots at the crossroads and decides to attack Jerusalem first, showing that God governs history.
The Ammonites, for gloating over Jerusalem's disaster, are also judged, for God will punish each in righteousness.
chapters.application: When we face hardship, let us examine whether we have strayed from God and turn back in time, for he is both righteous and full of mercy.

chapters.summary: Ezekiel declares that Jerusalem, for shedding blood, worshiping idols, and other sins, will be judged, and that God will refine and cleanse them.
keyPoints: It lists Jerusalem's sins: shedding blood, worshiping idols, dishonoring parents, and oppressing the sojourner.
Prophets, priests, princes, and people are all corrupt; God seeks someone to repair the wall's breach but finds no one.
God will judge them as metal is refined in a furnace, so that they may know that he is the LORD.
chapters.application: When wickedness spreads, God seeks those willing to stand in the gap. Let us examine ourselves, turn away from injustice, and become intercessors, keeping watch for our community and church.

chapters.summary: This chapter uses two sisters to represent Samaria and Jerusalem, describing the judgment they bring upon themselves through idol worship and alliances with foreign nations.
keyPoints: The two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, represent Samaria and Jerusalem, symbolizing spiritual whoredom.
They ally themselves with powerful nations such as Assyria and Babylon, and imitate their idol worship, leading to moral corruption.
God declares judgment, letting them be shamed and destroyed by those they loved, showing forth his righteousness and holiness.
chapters.application: Let us turn away from everything that would take God's place, remain faithful in our relationship with him, lest we fall into spiritual whoredom and come under his discipline.

chapters.summary: Through a parable God declares that Jerusalem will be destroyed, and instructs Ezekiel not to mourn for his dead wife, as a sign for the people of Israel.
keyPoints: Through the parable of the boiling pot, God declares that Jerusalem will be boiled away like meat in a pot, a sign that judgment is surely coming.
God commands Ezekiel not to mourn for his dead wife, as a sign that Israel will no longer mourn.
This chapter stresses that God's judgment will surely be fulfilled, so that the people may know that he is the LORD.
chapters.application: When suffering comes, let us wait quietly on God, trust that his will shall be accomplished, and learn obedience and trust through it.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the LORD's judgment against four nations - Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia - because they gloated over and took revenge on Judah; God will make their lands desolate to show that he is the LORD.
keyPoints: God judges the Ammonites for gloating over Judah's fall; their land becomes pastureland, so that all peoples may know him.
Moab and Edom are punished for their hatred of Judah; God stretches out his hand against them, bringing shame upon their borders.
The Philistines, for their lasting hatred and vengeance, are cut off by God, showing forth his justice.
chapters.application: When others suffer hardship, let us have compassion rather than gloat over their misfortune, for God examines the heart and will judge all peoples in righteousness; may we treat others with reverence, bringing glory to God.

chapters.summary: God declares that Tyre, for gloating over Jerusalem's downfall, will be besieged by many nations, overturned, and destroyed, becoming a desolate ruin that displays the majesty of God's judgment.
keyPoints: Tyre is judged for gloating over the disaster that befell Jerusalem.
God gathers many nations like waves of the sea to besiege Tyre, leaving it a bare rock.
Tyre's wealth, glory, and prosperity will come to nothing, and it will become a place where fishermen spread their nets.
chapters.application: When others meet with disaster, let us show compassion rather than gloat. Let us humbly rely on God, for he governs all things and will judge in righteousness.

chapters.summary: This chapter, in the form of a lament, portrays the splendor and downfall of Tyre, a picture of how the proud and self-reliant will surely fall.
keyPoints: Tyre is likened to a magnificent ship, built from the goods of many nations, a picture of her commercial wealth and power.
The ship is wrecked in the heart of the seas, and her rowers, sailors, and warriors are thrown into terror, picturing the loss of all her allies and resources.
The lament calls on the kings and merchants of the earth to tremble at Tyre's downfall, displaying the majesty of God's judgment.
chapters.application: Do not rely on wealth or power, but humbly trust in God. What we boast of today may be worthless tomorrow - only those who fear the LORD will be established.

chapters.summary: Ezekiel declares God's judgment on the king of Tyre for his pride in setting himself up as a god, laments his downfall, and foretells disaster on Sidon, closing with God's favor toward Israel.
keyPoints: The king of Tyre, grown proud through his great wisdom and wealth, regards himself as a god, and must be judged.
Through Ezekiel, God declares that though the king of Tyre once dwelt in Eden-like splendor, he is cast out for his sin, falling like a cherub.
God judges Sidon, removing its power to wound Israel like a thorn, displaying his holiness and justice.
chapters.application: Let us humble ourselves before God, acknowledging that all wisdom and wealth come from him, and not boast in ourselves. Let us serve him in reverence, turning away from pride, for God blesses the humble.

chapters.summary: Through Ezekiel, God declares judgment on Egypt for claiming the Nile as its own and oppressing Israel; Egypt will lie desolate for forty years.
keyPoints: God rebukes Pharaoh of Egypt, proud as a great crocodile, who will be hooked and cast out into the wilderness.
Egypt's land will lie desolate for forty years, its people scattered among the nations, before later being restored.
Egypt's downfall is so that Israel will no longer lean on Egypt, but will know that the LORD is God.
chapters.application: Do not rely on worldly power or your own cleverness, but humbly trust in God, for he governs all things and acts in righteousness.

chapters.summary: Through Ezekiel, God declares judgment on Egypt and its allies, leaving them desolate, to show that the LORD alone is the true God.
keyPoints: The day of the LORD draws near, and Egypt will face the sword, its people falling.
God will break Egypt's power and lay its land waste, so that they will know that he is the LORD.
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon will serve as God's instrument of judgment, plundering Egypt.
chapters.application: When the powers of this world seem unshakable, let us remember that God alone governs all things. In times of upheaval, let us humbly trust in him rather than in human strength.

chapters.summary: Using the image of the king of Assyria, this chapter describes him as a towering, magnificent cedar, cut down by God for his pride - a warning of what awaits Egypt.
keyPoints: Assyria is like a cedar of Lebanon, tall and beautiful beyond all other trees, yet cut down because its heart grew proud.
God hands Assyria over to the nations, cutting it off for its wickedness, so that the nations no longer rely on its power.
Though Egypt is mighty, it too will fall to the grave like Assyria, lying down with the uncircumcised.
chapters.application: Let us humbly rely on God rather than boast in our own talent or achievement, for all glory comes from him, and pride surely leads to downfall.

chapters.summary: This chapter is the LORD's lament over Pharaoh of Egypt, foretelling that he will fall into the grave together with many nations, showing God's judgment and the fate of the nations.
keyPoints: Through the prophet Ezekiel, God laments over Egypt, likening Pharaoh to a great crocodile and declaring that he will be caught.
God will bring down Egypt and all its people by the swords of many nations, cutting off its power and shaking the ends of the earth.
Egypt will go down to the grave, lying with the uncircumcised nations, suffering shame and the sword.
chapters.application: Let us humbly rely on God and never oppress the weak by our strength, for God will surely judge pride. May we examine ourselves daily, turn away from self-righteousness, and live in reverence before him.

chapters.summary: This chapter tells how God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman, declaring both personal responsibility and God's justice, and calls Israel to repent and return to him.
keyPoints: God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman; if he fails to warn the wicked, their blood will be required of him.
God's justice is impartial: the righteous who turn from righteousness will die, and the wicked who turn from wickedness will live.
Though Israel comes to inquire with their lips, their hearts still cling to sin, and God will judge them by their deeds.
chapters.application: Let us stay watchful before God, keeping watch for ourselves and others, and repent sincerely, turning from sin to live a life worthy of our faith.

chapters.summary: This chapter condemns Israel's shepherds for failing their duty, and promises that God himself will seek out and shepherd his flock, setting up David as their shepherd and making a covenant of peace with them.
keyPoints: Israel's shepherds care only for themselves and fail to feed the flock, causing the sheep to be scattered.
God himself will be their shepherd, seeking out the lost, binding up the injured, and feeding them with justice.
God will set up David as their shepherd, making with them a covenant of peace, so that Israel will be blessed.
chapters.application: Let us examine whether we are fulfilling our own duty to shepherd others, and let us trust in God, our good shepherd - he will watch over us and lead us into peace and restoration.

chapters.summary: God declares judgment on Edom for its hatred of Israel; its land will become desolate, showing that God is the Lord over all.
keyPoints: God commands Ezekiel to face Mount Seir and prophesy, declaring that Edom will be repaid.
Because Edom nursed an ancient hatred and took advantage of Israel's disaster, God will repay it according to its deeds.
Edom's land becomes a desolate waste, empty of both people and livestock, so that all will know that the LORD is God.
chapters.application: Let us remember that God is a righteous judge; let us not repay evil with evil, but hold to a heart of love, for God will repay every person according to their deeds.

chapters.summary: God promises to give the people of Israel a new heart and a new spirit, bringing them back to their own land and bringing glory to his holy name.
keyPoints: God rebukes Edom and the surrounding nations for plundering Israel, and declares judgment upon them.
For the sake of his holy name, God blesses Israel, cleanses them, and settles them once again in their land.
God promises to give them a new heart and a new spirit, so that they will keep his statutes and become his own people.
chapters.application: When we feel we have failed or drifted from God, let us remember his promise of a new heart and a new spirit - by his grace, we can begin again and live a life of obedience.

chapters.summary: This chapter records God's vision to Ezekiel of the valley of dry bones coming to life, a picture of how the whole house of Israel will return from exile and be given new life.
keyPoints: God leads the prophet to a valley full of dry bones and asks whether they can live again; the prophet answers, O Lord GOD, you know.
God commands the prophet to prophesy: bone joins to bone, sinews, flesh, and skin cover them, breath enters them, and they become a vast army.
Two sticks joined into one foreshadow the reunion of Judah and Israel; God sets up David's descendant as king and makes an everlasting covenant with them.
chapters.application: When life feels as dry and hopeless as these bones, God can still breathe new life into it. May we declare his promises in faith, seeing his work even in despair, and live in the hope of resurrection.

chapters.summary: Through the prophet Ezekiel, the LORD foretells that in the last days many nations will gather to attack Israel, but God himself will judge them, displaying his holiness and sovereignty.
keyPoints: It is foretold that Gog will form an alliance with many nations and come from the north against Israel like a cloud covering the land.
God allows this attack to happen so that his glory may be displayed and the nations may know that he is the one true God.
God judges the enemy with earthquake, plague, and sword, protecting his people and showing forth his faithfulness.
chapters.application: In the face of the world's turmoil, let us trust in God's sovereignty - he will protect those who belong to him. Let us stay watchful in prayer, live faithfully, and give him the glory.

chapters.summary: God declares judgment on Gog, bringing about his total defeat, and displays his holy name through the cleansing and restoration of Israel.
keyPoints: God destroys Gog and his army with bow and arrow, torrential rain, fire, and burning sulfur.
The people of Israel burn the enemy's weapons for fuel for seven years, cleansing the holy land.
God brings the exiled Israelites home, pours out his Spirit upon them, and shows himself holy.
chapters.application: In the midst of hardship, let us remember that God governs all things - his judgment is righteous and his promises will surely be fulfilled. May we wait in faith for his deliverance and live in holiness.

chapters.summary: In a vision, Ezekiel sees the detailed dimensions and structure of the temple, a picture of God's promise of restoration and presence.
keyPoints: In the vision, God reveals to Ezekiel the blueprint of the temple, emphasizing divine order and precision.
The temple's measurements show how much God values worship, requiring that it be built exactly to specification.
This chapter opens the vision of the temple's rebuilding, foreshadowing Israel's restoration and God's presence with them.
chapters.application: Let us treat God's house with reverence, seeking order and holiness in our worship and daily life, confident that God will surely restore us.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes in detail the structure and dimensions of the temple's interior as Ezekiel saw it in the vision, emphasizing God's glory and holiness.
keyPoints: The dimensions and structure of the temple's outer room, inner room, and Most Holy Place are described.
Side chambers surround the temple walls in three stories, each wider than the one below, used for service and storage.
Carvings of cherubim and palm trees decorate the temple, symbols of God's glory and life.
chapters.application: God cares about every detail of his temple, just as he cares about every part of our lives. May we build our own hearts as a sanctuary with reverence, giving God first place.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes the prophet, in the vision, measuring the chambers around the temple that were used by the priests, displaying God's holiness and order.
keyPoints: The prophet is led to the chambers facing north in the outer court and measures their dimensions, showing the precision of the temple's design.
The holy chambers rise in three stories, each upper story narrower than the one below because the galleries take up space, reflecting the skill of the design.
These chambers are set apart for the priests to eat the most holy offerings, to store their holy garments, and to reside in, underscoring their consecrated office.
chapters.application: Let us worship God with reverence, keeping order in our daily lives and holding to holiness, for God is holy, and he calls us to be holy as well.

chapters.summary: In the vision, the prophet Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD return to the temple, and he receives the law concerning the altar and its sacrifices.
keyPoints: The glory of the LORD returns through the east gate and fills the whole temple, showing that God is willing to dwell among his people.
God gives instructions for the temple's law, stressing that the house of Israel must put away idolatry and unfaithfulness, and be restored to holiness.
The dimensions of the altar and the regulations for sacrifice are laid out in detail, foreshadowing the restoration of ordered worship.
chapters.application: God longs to dwell within us. Let us cleanse ourselves and clothe ourselves with holiness, so that his glory may fill our lives.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the closing of the temple's east gate in Jerusalem and the rules for worship, stressing the holiness and duties of the priests and Levites.
keyPoints: The east gate is shut, and only the prince may sit within it, a sign of God's holiness and glory.
The Levites are punished for straying from God and are barred from serving before him, allowed only to keep watch at the temple gates.
The priests must wear linen garments and not shave their heads, teaching the people to distinguish the holy from the common.
chapters.application: Let us worship God with reverence, hold to holiness in every area of life, and faithfully carry out the duties he has entrusted to us.

chapters.summary: This chapter lays out the allotment of the holy land and the area around the temple, along with the responsibilities of the prince and the people in offerings and festivals.
keyPoints: A portion of holy land is set apart for the LORD, including the temple and the land for the priests.
The Levites' towns and the land surrounding them are also allotted.
The prince is to act justly and righteously, and provide the offerings for the people.
chapters.application: Let us order our lives around God, pursue fairness and holiness in everything, and give willingly to support God's house.

chapters.summary: This chapter gives detailed instructions for temple worship, including the offerings for the sabbath and the new moon, along with the prince's duties and the people's manner of worship.
keyPoints: On the sabbath and the new moon, the east gate is opened; the prince worships at the gateway while the people worship at the entrance.
The prince is to provide burnt offerings and peace offerings, presenting them on behalf of the people at the appointed feasts.
When the people come to worship at the sanctuary, they enter by the north gate and leave by the south gate, keeping proper order.
chapters.application: In worship, let us keep proper order, prepare our hearts, draw near to God in reverence, and faithfully fulfill our own role in life.

chapters.summary: In the vision, Ezekiel sees water flowing out from the temple, growing deeper and deeper, bringing life and healing - a picture of how God's presence brings abundance and renewal.
keyPoints: Water flows out from beneath the threshold of the temple, growing from a trickle into a great river.
Everywhere the river flows, life springs up, fish teem in abundance, and even the Dead Sea is healed.
Fruit trees line the riverbanks, their leaves never withering, their fruit serving as food and their leaves for healing.
chapters.application: May we often come to God's house, letting the living water of the Spirit nourish our hearts, so that our lives bear good fruit and become a blessing to others.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes the allotment of land to each tribe of Israel around the holy portion, and the holiness of the city of Jerusalem and God's presence within it.
keyPoints: Seven tribes receive their allotment in the north, each tribe's portion stretching from east to west.
The central portion is the holy offering, including the land for the priests and Levites and the holy city.
The remaining five tribes receive their allotment in the south; the city has twelve gates, and its name is 'The LORD Is There.'
chapters.application: God has prepared a beautiful dwelling place for his people. Let us clothe ourselves with holiness and always remember his presence, giving him first place in every area of life.
